S1 camera outage (90 days, 9 cameras, fu.assumptions: failure prob 0.01/camera-day, duration uniform (1, 2, 3) days, busiest-site share 0.18 of citywide reads
S1 camera outage (90 days, 9 cameras, fu.reading: one week dark at the busiest site costs ~1.6x an average site and ~5 expected matches — the matches are not delayed, they are gone; the vehicle does not come back.

S2 backhaul drop / store-and-forward (18.assumptions: actionable window 600 s after the read; normal latency lognormal median 25 s sigma 0.8; per-site outage 2%/site-day, uniform 1-8 h
S2 backhaul drop / store-and-forward (18.reading: store-and-forward preserves the RECORD perfectly and the ALERT barely at all: a queued hot-list alert is a Tier 2 lead by the time it lands. The design must show read age on every alert and never present a stale alert as live.

S3 disk pressure (9 cameras, full volume.assumptions: 170 KB retained per read (snapshot + crop), disk 500 GB, base system 60 GB, retention failure begins day 30 at plateau
S3 disk pressure (9 cameras, full volume.(b) retention dead, NO alarm: use after: 219 GB; disk 100% full on day 74 (500 GB) or day 41 (250 GB)
S3 disk pressure (9 cameras, full volume.reading: the 14-day retention IS the disk-sizing control. On a 500 GB disk an unnoticed dead retention job takes ~6 weeks to fill the disk; on a 250 GB disk ~2 weeks. The dead-man alarm converts both into a rounding error — but only if something off the box notices the silence (see TRACK-C-REPORT findings).

S4 clock skew (two cameras, one day, ~9,.assumptions: camera B clock offset fixed per run; events are Poisson streams at the Cabot per-camera rate (mean gap 17.5 s/read)
S4 clock skew (two cameras, one day, ~9,.reads/day/camera retained PAST the 14-da: 34 reads, each up to 10 min over policy
S4 clock skew (two cameras, one day, ~9,.reads/day/camera deleted EARLY on a +10: 34 (non-hit reads; verified hits are held separately and unaffected)
S4 clock skew (two cameras, one day, ~9,.chain effect: none — Sentinel appends in server-receipt order; a bad camera clock cannot rewrite or reorder the chain
S4 clock skew (two cameras, one day, ~9,.reading: at Cabot's per-camera rate, reads arrive every ~17 s, so even a +30 s skew — well inside what an undisciplined camera clock drifts to — inverts a visible share of a two-camera evidence timeline. Retention must key on server receipt time, and skew must be measured by camera NTP discipline, not inferred from arrivals (S2 shows arrivals can legitimately be hours late).

S5 OCR degradation + false-alert base ra.assumptions: rain accuracy day 0.90 / night 0.84 (new); rain 15% of hours; alert verification takes 3 min of an officer's time per alert
S5 OCR degradation + false-alert base ra.false-alert rate 0.01% -> per day city: 4.44 false alerts/day, 13 min/day of verification time
S5 OCR degradation + false-alert base ra.reading: weather costs a handful of missed passes; the false-alert rate costs the whole alert queue. At 0.1% false, officers would verify ~12 false alerts for every true one and the verify-before-stop step — the control everything else rests on — becomes the thing a tired operator starts skipping. The pilot accuracy protocol must measure the false-alert rate per 100k reads, not just OCR accuracy.

S6 hot-list staleness, 48 h sync outage.assumptions: list churn 2%/day of 220 entries removed upstream
S6 hot-list staleness, 48 h sync outage.FAIL OPEN: expected stale-list alerts (r: 0.30 per outage; simulated mean 0.24; P(at least one) 22% over 300 simulated outages
S6 hot-list staleness, 48 h sync outage.FAIL CLOSED: legitimate queries blocked: Tier 2 8 + Tier 3 applications 1 = 9 delayed (not lost — they re-run when sync returns); stale alerts 0
S6 hot-list staleness, 48 h sync outage.reading: fail-closed converts a safety failure (acting on a recalled warrant) into an availability cost (expected ~13 delayed queries per 48 h outage — 9 in this seeded run — each recoverable). Fail-open is silent until the day it isn't: most outages produce no stale alert, which is exactly why the failure would go unnoticed until one does. That asymmetry is why the design fails closed.

S7 emergency-flag normalization (K8).assumptions: emergency use creeps +5%/month compounded from 2.6999999999999997/month baseline; K8 threshold operationalized as emergencies > 25% of Tier 3 actions in a month
S7 emergency-flag normalization (K8).reading: 5%/month creep is invisible month to month and trips K8 in under two years. Nothing about the creep announces itself — K8 only fires if the monthly report COMPUTES the emergency share. A kill condition nobody calculates is not a kill condition.

S8 full run -> \u00a7 12-12-1805 six-mon.assumption: prosecutions = 45% of arrests filed in-period (no Cabot source; the number must come from a prosecutor feedback loop in production — see findings)
S8 full run -> \u00a7 12-12-1805 six-mon.true hot-list passes drawn (pre-OCR) vs: 663 vs 688 (8.25/100k vs the 8.56 anchor — this is the like-for-like line)
S8 full run -> \u00a7 12-12-1805 six-mon.confirmed matches per list: arrest warrant: 160; custom (gated): 56; missing / endangered: 89; stolen plate: 103; stolen vehicle: 217
S8 full run -> \u00a7 12-12-1805 six-mon.report identical after purge: True (built from counters + plate-free outcomes only; outcome records carry no plate and no plate_ref)

S9 legal-hold lifecycle.reading: retention is not a timer on evidence. The hit survived four deletion attempts across four states and was deleted exactly once — after export, sign-off, and release, each step chained.
